chapter_theme: The kaathai of setting up the household: in Puhar's inexhaustible wealth the newly married Kannaki and Kovalan, likened to those who enjoy in Uttarakuru the fruit of completed austerity, climb to the terrace of their mansion on a spring evening; Kovalan pours out an unmeasured praise that has the gods surrender their weapons to her body and asks why her maids adorned a beauty that needs nothing; then an elder lady sets Kannaki up in a household of her own for charity and the hosting of guests, some years pass, and a closing venba says the two enjoyed every pleasure inseparably, as if they had seen that nothing on earth lasts.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, daughter of the merchant Maanaaygan
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband
the great lady of the house who sets Kannaki up in a household of her own; the unit does not name her, and the story suggests an elder of the family, likely Kovalan's mother

silappathikaram:2:1-11.reading: The narrator describes Puhar, city of famed merchants, so rich that its stores would not run short if the whole sea-girt world came to it, filled with rare goods brought by ship and cart, home of wealthy houses that never fall from their lineage, and there sets the flower-eyed bride and her loving husband, who appear like those who completed hard austerity and are born to enjoy in Uttarakuru.
silappathikaram:2:1-11.nuance: The couple's happiness is introduced through a simile of reward: Uttarakuru is the land where the fruit of austerity is enjoyed (அருந்தவம் முடித்தோர்), so the marriage is pictured as a store of merit being spent, and what is spent can run out. The unit is the subject of a sentence that runs on to line 37 without a main verb; the couple are named only by epithets (கயமலர்க் கண்ணியும் காதல் கொழுநனும்).

claims.claim: those who complete hard austerity are born again to enjoy a land of plenty such as Uttarakuru

silappathikaram:2:12-27.reading: Seated on a jewelled couch like Maya's work in the middle storey of their tall mansion, the couple see the fragrant southern breeze enter through the latticed window with bees that have fed on the field flowers and on the thaazhai, the maadhavi creeper and the champak grove, and delighted and deepened in love they climb to the open terrace where spring sits enthroned with its arrows of flowers.
silappathikaram:2:12-27.nuance: Spring with its flower-arrows (விரைமலர் வாளியொடு வேனில்) is the love god's season, so the breeze is a messenger of desire. Among the scents it carries is the மாதவி creeper (line 18), the same name the dancer bears who will take Kovalan from this house in the next kaathai; the text does not point to it, and the echo may be no more than a reader's.
silappathikaram:2:12-27.event: Kovalan and Kannaki, delighted by the spring breeze in their chamber, climb to the terrace of their mansion.

silappathikaram:2:28-52.reading: On the flower bed Kovalan paints sugarcane and creeper on her shoulders, the two shine together like sun and moon lighting the world, their garlands tangle, and gazing at her face in love he speaks: the great god should give her the crescent moon he wears as her brow, since it is her sibling; the bodiless god gave his cane bow as her two brows; the king of gods gave the middle of his thunderbolt as her waist, since she appeared before the nectar; and the six-faced god gave his one spear as her two eyes.
silappathikaram:2:28-52.nuance: Lines 28 to 37 are the narrator's and the speech begins at 38. The praise makes the gods hand over their weapons, as one gives arms to a champion at the front (lines 42-43), so her body is imagined as an armoury that conquers; the moon being her sibling and her appearing before the nectar both suggest she is likened to Lakshmi, born of the churned sea, though the text does not name her. Line 37 calls the speech குறியாக் கட்டுரை, an unmeasured or unconsidered speech, which may judge Kovalan's excess as well as describe it.
silappathikaram:2:28-52.event: Kovalan paints his bride's shoulders and begins a long praise of her beauty.
silappathikaram:2:28-52.unit_note: End moved from line 50 to line 52: the question about the six-faced god's spear, begun at line 49, closes with ஈத்தது? on line 52.

silappathikaram:2:53-72.reading: Kovalan goes on: the peacock beaten by her grace has fled to the forest, the swan beaten by her gait hides among the lotus pools, and the parrot, pained by her prattle that is sweeter than flute, lute and nectar, still will not leave her hand; then he asks why those who praise her beauty decked her with ornaments beyond the auspicious one, with garlands beyond the flowers of her hair, musk beyond incense, and a strand of pearls beyond the painting on her breasts, making her small waist suffer.
silappathikaram:2:53-72.nuance: The parrot is pitied (அளிய தாமே) because it loses to her and still stays, unlike the peacock and swan that withdraw; the catalogue of adornments turns into a reproach of her attendants, the convention that beauty is burdened by what is added to it. The faultless auspicious ornament (மறுஇல் மங்கல அணி, line 63) is the one ornament he allows, the wife's mark, set against the rest.
silappathikaram:2:53-72.unit_note: Start moved from line 51 to 53 (see the previous unit) and end from line 66 to 72: the run of questions about her ornaments, begun at line 62, ends with என்உற் றனர்க்கொல்? on line 72.

silappathikaram:2:73-90.reading: Kovalan calls her flawless gold, pearl of the right-whorled conch, pure fragrance, sugarcane, honey, rare doll, medicine of his life, innocent daughter of the great merchant house, and asks whether to call her a gem not born of mountains, nectar not born of the sea, music not born of the lute; so he delights with her, and as the days go the great lady of the house, wishing to see Kannaki's charity and her household that welcomes guests flourish, sets her up apart with her own retinue, and some years pass for Kannaki in the dignity of the house.
silappathikaram:2:73-90.nuance: Lines 73 to 80 are Kovalan's words, closed by என்று at line 80; from line 81 the narrator speaks. The title's மனையறம் is given its content here: the household is set up so that its charity (அறப் பரிசாரம்) and hospitality (விருந்து புறந்தருஉம்) may be seen, which is the life Kannaki will later say she has lost. 'Some years passed' (யாண்டுசில கழிந்தன) closes the happy time in four words. Who the great lady is the unit does not say.
silappathikaram:2:73-90.event: After Kovalan's praise, an elder lady of the family sets Kannaki up in a household of her own, and some years pass.

claims.claim: a household is set up for charity and the welcoming of guests

silappathikaram:2:73-90.unit_note: Start moved from line 67 to 73: the questions about her ornaments end at line 72, and the run of endearments that the narrator closes with என்று at line 80 begins at line 73.

silappathikaram:2:91-94.reading: A closing venba says that the two, joined like intertwined serpents and never parting, hand in hand as husband and wife, enjoyed every pleasure whose name does not fade, standing on the earth like people who had seen its impermanence.
silappathikaram:2:91-94.nuance: The last line turns the knowledge of impermanence into a reason for haste in pleasure rather than for renunciation, as the ethics books use it; the simile 'as if they had seen' (கண்டவர்ப்போல்) leaves open whether they did see it. ஒருவார், 'they did not part', is undone in the next kaathai. The image of தூமப் பணிகள் (smoky or dark serpents coiled together) is not certain in its first word.

links.note: The couplet asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on the beloved's soft arms; the epic likens the newly married couple to those who enjoy in Uttarakuru the fruit of completed austerity.
links.teaches: Both weigh a couple's joy against a heavenly world, but the couplet ranks love above heaven while the epic makes the couple's joy itself a heaven earned by past austerity, and so something that can be used up, which is how the epic prepares its turn from pleasure to karma.

gains.a: the epic's simile gains a contrast: love here is not set above heaven but counted as heaven's wage, a measure of merit rather than a rival to it
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question gains an answer it does not give, that the beloved's arms may be a heaven only for as long as the merit behind them lasts

links.note: The couplet says the woman who wore anicham flowers with their stems will hear no good drums for her waist; Kovalan asks why her attendants loaded her with garland, musk and pearls, making her small waist suffer.
links.teaches: The epic takes the Kural's single joke of a waist too fine to bear flowers and spreads it over a whole toilette, moving the lover's praise from the secret meeting into the marriage chamber, where it is the husband who speaks it and the maids who are blamed.

gains.a: Kovalan's catalogue gains a known convention behind it, so its reproach of the attendants reads as praise in the established form of நலம்புனைந்துரைத்தல்
gains.b: the couplet gains a speaker and setting it lacks, a husband in the first days of marriage, showing the convention used outside the lovers' secret union

links.note: The elder lady sets Kannaki up in a household for charity and the hosting of guests; in Madurai Kannaki says she has lost giving to the virtuous, tending Brahmins, receiving ascetics and welcoming guests.
links.teaches: The household the second kaathai founds for its charity and hospitality is named, duty by duty, as what Kannaki has lost, so the pair shows her grief in Madurai as the loss of a household's dharma, not only of a husband's company.

links.note: In the bridal chamber Kovalan calls Kannaki gold and doll (பொன்னே, பாவாய்) for her beauty; in Madurai, after she has followed him, he calls her gold, creeper and doll of modesty for the steadfastness that brought her with him.
links.teaches: The same endearments return with a new ground: the words that praised her body in the chamber praise her chastity and endurance on the road, so the pair traces Kovalan's turn from admiring Kannaki's beauty to recognising her virtue.

links.note: The couplet says all of keeping a house is for tending guests and doing good; the epic's household is set up so that its charity and hospitality may be seen, and the story later takes both away.
links.teaches: The epic founds Kannaki's household on exactly the couplet's purpose, then lets a husband's absence and exile empty it, showing that the householder's dharma the couplet assigns to the house depends on the pair staying in it.

gains.a: the narrator's brief line on the household's purpose gains the weight of a stated rule, so its later loss reads as the loss of the household's whole reason
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a case of its failure: a wife ready to keep it who cannot once her husband leaves the house

links.note: The quatrain mocks one who sees a corpse carried to the burning ground yet marries and thinks there is joy here; the venba says the newly married couple enjoyed every pleasure like people who had seen the world's impermanence.
links.teaches: The same knowledge that nothing on earth lasts is, for the Naladiyar, a reason to give up marriage and its joys and, in the epic's venba, a reason to take them while they last, so the pair sets out the two lessons impermanence can teach.

gains.a: the venba's last line gains a rival reading of its own premise, so its haste for pleasure is seen as a choice the ethics book condemns
gains.b: the quatrain gains the voice it argues against: not a fool blind to death but lovers who claim to have seen it and draw the opposite lesson

links.note: The venba says husband and wife, joined like coiled serpents, never parted; in the next kaathai Kovalan buys Madhavi's garland, cannot leave her and forgets his home.
links.teaches: The closing praise of a union that never parts is reversed within one kaathai, and the venba's own hint of impermanence turns out to be about the marriage itself rather than about the world.

source_issues: The edition prints 90 as the last line: the count covers the akaval (lines 1-90) and leaves out the closing venba (91-94).
Line 72 has என்உற் றனர்க்கொல் with a doubled க், against என்உற் றனர்கொல் on line 66; probably a misprint.
Lines 62 and 73-75 carry full stops after vocatives (கோதை.நின், பொன்னே., முத்தே.), editorial punctuation for exclamation; line 62 lacks a space after the stop.
Lines 49-50 (பெறுமுறை இன்றியும் இறுமுறை காணும் இயல்பினின்) are hard to construe, so the reason given for the six-faced god's gift is uncertain.
Line 91: the sense of தூமப் பணிகள் (smoky or dark serpents) is not certain.
